name: Social skills / game / pickup

lead: 'Game' is the pickup community's term for skills in meeting and attracting partners, split into inner game (confidence, psychology) and outer game (social skills, fitness, fashion, grooming). In looksmaxxing it is often discussed as a complement to appearance, to turn good looks into actual attraction.

The chain is practising social skills and confidence, building the outer game of fitness, style and grooming, and arriving at stronger presence. It spread through online forums from the 1990s and reached the mainstream with Neil Strauss's 2005 book The Game. Some commentators say there is no evidence its claims work, while others say principles such as generating attraction and building rapport have some support in social and evolutionary psychology.

paras: Practitioners approach people repeatedly, practise conversation, and follow staged sequences from attraction to comfort. Many buy workshops, books or coaching, and combine it with gym, style and grooming work. Some schools use NLP-derived methods, which scientific consensus treats as pseudoscience.

Critics describe parts of the movement as sexist or misogynistic, and the Southern Poverty Law Center characterises it as male supremacist. Specific tactics such as 'negging' and last-minute-resistance techniques have drawn criticism, and some instructors have faced travel bans after videos of unwanted physical contact.

chain: Better outer game: fitness, style, grooming
angle.text: Pickup communities teach inner game (confidence) and outer game (fitness, fashion, grooming) so looks translate into attraction. Some principles have academic support, the community draws strong criticism, and effectiveness claims have not been tested.

lead: Social skills, 'game' and pickup are the names for learning how to meet, talk to and attract romantic or sexual partners. Practitioners treat attractiveness as more than facial structure: inner game covers confidence, self-esteem and mindset, while outer game covers conversation, body language, fitness, fashion and grooming.[1] For looksmaxxers this is the presentation layer, the way an improved face, physique and wardrobe get noticed and turned into actual connection, and practitioners hold that these skills improve with repetition.[1]

The modern pickup scene traces to 1960s and 1970s how-to books, to Ross Jeffries's 'speed seduction' workshops from 1988, and to the alt.seduction.fast newsgroup founded in 1994.[1][2] Journalist Neil Strauss's 2005 book The Game and the VH1 series The Pick Up Artist (2007 to 2008) carried it to a mass audience, and it has since become a commercial market of workshops, books, video courses and online coaching.[1][3]

Looksmaxxing forums run their own social-skills threads, including multi-part series on body language and social psychology, alongside a recurring argument about how much conversation skill matters next to looks.[4][5][6][7] Commentators disagree about pickup's merits. Psychologist Petra Boynton said in 2010 that there was no evidence of effectiveness, while Oesch and Miklousic (2012) reviewed the literature and found partial support in social and evolutionary psychology for principles such as generating attraction and building rapport.[1] Critics, including the Southern Poverty Law Center, describe the movement as sexist or male supremacist, and several of its best-known figures have been the subject of public controversy.[1][8]

paras: Pickup practitioners call their body of technique 'game' and their network the seduction community. Wikipedia describes it as a largely heterosexual male subculture whose members study psychology and behaviour in order to meet and attract women.[1] Inner game refers to confidence, self-esteem and the psychological side; outer game refers to social skill, fitness, fashion and grooming.[1] That second half overlaps directly with looksmaxxing, which is why the two communities share vocabulary and members.

The community separates four settings. Day game means approaching people on streets, in parks and in shops; night game means bars and clubs; message game means dating apps and social media; and social-circle game means parties, universities and workplaces.[1] Approaches are described as indirect, beginning with casual conversation, or direct, openly signalling interest.[1] Approach anxiety, the fear of rejection that stops people starting conversations, is treated as a central obstacle, and many programmes are built around repeated, graduated practice at starting conversations.[1]

Wikipedia traces the genre to The Art of Erotic Seduction (1967), by psychotherapist Albert Ellis and Roger Conway, and to Eric Weber's How to Pick Up Girls! (1970).[1] Ross Jeffries began studying seduction in 1988 and taught workshops on what he called speed seduction, a method based on neuro-linguistic programming that aims to guide a woman's imagination towards a desired emotional state.[1][2] He appeared on talk shows from 1992 onward and is called the 'godfather' of the modern community in Strauss's book.[2] Filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson said Tom Cruise's character in Magnolia (1999) was inspired by Jeffries, although Cruise denied it.[1][2]

In 1994 Lewis DePayne, a former Jeffries student, founded the alt.seduction.fast newsgroup, which led to a network of forums, email lists and blogs; in the late 1990s Clifford Lee's Cliff's List Seduction Letter became an independent voice, and local study groups developed into 'lairs' combining online forums with in-person meetings.[1] The community's shared vocabulary, including 'sets', 'indicators of interest' and 'kino', was built in these spaces.[1]

Erik von Markovik, known as Mystery, was born in Toronto in 1971 and created his persona in the late 1990s for mentalist and magic performances. He published The Venusian Arts Handbook (2005) and, with Chris Odom, The Mystery Method (2006), which described approaching a group, giving attention to everyone in it, and then focusing on a target.[1][9] Strauss's own immersion began in 2001 under the pseudonym 'Style'; he wrote a 2004 New York Times article and then The Game (2005), which reached the Times bestseller list and No. 1 on Amazon.[1][3][10] Former participants of the Project Hollywood house described in the book went on to found Real Social Dynamics.[3]

The Game, published in September 2005, follows Strauss as he joins online discussion groups, attends a boot camp run by Mystery, adopts the persona 'Style' and moves into a shared house called Project Hollywood, whose collapse amid rivalries ends the story. Strauss concludes in the book that a life devoted only to picking up women is unfulfilling and recommends a more balanced life.[3] It spent two months on the New York Times bestseller list and regained attention in 2007 with VH1's The Pick Up Artist, hosted by Mystery.[3][9] Film rights were optioned by Sony in 2006 and passed through several studios in the following decade.[3]

Reviews were mixed. Steven Poole in The Guardian noted that the techniques can lower a practitioner's view of women; Rafael Behr in The Observer called some techniques, such as the 'neg', sinister; Alexandra Jacobs in the New York Times said the author alternated between misogynistic remarks and weak self-awareness.[3] Strauss followed with Rules of the Game (2007), a more practical companion, and The Truth (2015), a memoir about the difficulty of long-term relationships after his years in the scene. In 2015 he said that some community members were damaged people with distorted, hateful views, and he has continued pickup-related coaching through Stylelife Academy, founded in 2007.[10]

Named techniques include the 'set' (a group of strangers approached, with attention given to all members before a target is chosen), the 'false time constraint' (a stated reason for having limited time, used so the approach does not seem needy), 'kino' (gradually escalating touch), 'pawning' (introducing an unwanted person to a friend as a display of social value) and 'going caveman' (more physical contact, less talk).[1] 'Negging', a backhanded compliment, is described by Strauss as aimed mainly at disqualifying the man as a suitor rather than lowering the woman's confidence; critics read it differently.[1] 'Last-minute resistance' tactics concern responding after a woman has said she does not want to have sex, and Wikipedia notes that these range from mutually respectful approaches to manipulation and rape.[1]

Jeffries's school drew on neuro-linguistic programming. NLP was introduced by Richard Bandler and John Grinder in the 1970s, and reviews since the 1980s have found little support for its core assumptions; researchers generally describe it as pseudoscience. Later instructors dropped many of Jeffries's claims while keeping some NLP elements.[1][11]

Looksmaxxing's usual framework treats the face, body and style as inputs and social outcomes as the output, so social-skills material sits at the end of that chain: forum members discuss how conversation, humour, posture and confidence determine whether an improved appearance leads to dates or friendships. On looksmax.org this appears as multi-part guides on personality types, body language and social psychology.[12][6][5] One guide for younger members advises relaxed posture, slow and controlled speech, small gestures and humour tied to the other person's interests, and describes being observant of cues.[13]

Threads such as 'women like guys with good social skills' and 'looks and social skills matter most in scenarios involving new people' argue that conversational ability and looks work together.[14][7] Others hold that looks are what make social skills pay off, or that there is little point improving looks without social skills.[15][16] A thread of pickup lines claimed to have worked in cold approaches shows the forum also trades anecdotes from street approaches.[17] T Nation members have discussed 'game' too, including a long thread in which a poster describes an instructor whose approach rests on confidence and humour.[18]

Wikipedia places pickup artistry among the core groups of the wider manosphere, alongside men's rights activists, incels and MGTOW, and describes The Game as a keystone work of that milieu. The shared 'alpha' and 'beta' vocabulary and the red-pill metaphor are common to several of these groups, which is part of why looksmaxxing and pickup discussions overlap and why critics sometimes treat them together.[19]

No study has tested pickup training itself as an intervention. Academic work on the community is mostly descriptive. Eric Hendriks (2012), drawing on boot camps and lairs in Germany, argued that successful practitioners combine hedonistic goals with disciplinarian and ascetic values, even though gurus often market a quick fix.[1] A McGill University ethnographic study by Rob Whitley and JunWei Zhou (2020) in Montreal found that men joined to address psychosocial deficits and to gain social skills, while participants also acknowledged a dark side.[1] Andrew King (2018) described the philosophy as paralleling the rise of feminism and as a critique of its limits.[1]

Nathan Oesch and Igor Miklousic (2012) reviewed the field in Evolutionary Psychology and concluded that some principles, such as generating attraction and building rapport, have partial support in social, physiological and evolutionary psychology.[1] Psychologist Petra Boynton said in 2010 that claims of effectiveness had no evidence behind them.[1]

Related research on social skills training comes from other settings. A 2025 meta-analysis of studies in children with autism reported small to moderate improvements in social communication, reciprocity and joint attention,[20] a 2011 meta-analysis of loneliness interventions found the most successful randomised studies addressed maladaptive social cognition,[21] and a 2014 review covers social skills training in child psychiatry.[22] These studies concern clinical groups rather than pickup.

The Southern Poverty Law Center classifies the movement as male supremacist, and a UCLA centre placed pickup culture on a continuum of sexist attitudes.[1] Clarisse Thorn, a feminist writer, called the community often absurd and sexist while arguing that its tactics reflect wider patterns in sexual behaviour; Gene Weingarten, who attended a Mystery Method seminar in 2008, questioned the ethics of institutionally taught seduction.[1] Defenders compared pickup to gym workouts or push-up bras, and Strauss said techniques can be used for good or evil.[1] A blogger profiled in 2006 offered the credo 'Leave her better than you found her.'[1]

In November 2014 Julien Blanc, then an instructor with Real Social Dynamics, became the subject of an online campaign, #TakeDownJulienBlanc, after videos showed him grabbing women by the neck. His Australian visa was revoked on 6 November, the UK denied him entry on 19 November, and Singapore announced a bar on 26 November; a petition against him gathered more than 330,000 signatures against a counter-petition of about 3,500 in his favour. He apologised on CNN, calling the videos a 'horrible attempt at humor' taken out of context, and later toured with his own self-help seminars.[8] Some outlets connected the wider manosphere to the 2014 Isla Vista killings, and researchers describe the manosphere's ideology as misogynistic and linked to online harassment and radicalisation.[1][19]

Many classic forums and lairs have gone offline. Wikipedia reports that the scene now operates mainly on Telegram, where groups such as Game Global help members find wingmen in more than 300 cities, and that Game Global declared pickup forums dead in January 2025.[1] Self-published authors such as Roosh V, whom Salon called the movement's cash cow, built a separate commercial line of books; Wikipedia notes he later renounced parts of his past and became an Orthodox Christian.[1] In 2026 Mystery released an ebook written with an AI companion he says he created.[9]
No studies found testing pickup training as an intervention. See the research section for descriptive and related studies.[1][20][21][22]
